scenes.heading: Database Migrations
scenes.narration: A database schema evolves over time, and every change must be versioned, reproducible, and applied in the same order everywhere. Let's make that safe.

scenes.heading: Why versioned migrations exist
items: Ad-hoc SQL run by hand causes schema drift
Each change gets an ordered version number
A tracking table records which versions have run
scenes.narration: Your schema is code: it changes as features land, and those changes must apply identically on every machine. Running SQL by hand drifts — one server gets a column another lacks. Migration tools give each change an ordered version and record the applied versions in a tracking table, so any database can be brought to a known state deterministically.

scenes.heading: How a migration run works
steps: Read the current version from the tracking table
Apply only the pending ones in order
Update the version as each succeeds
Mark dirty if one fails mid-way
scenes.narration: At deploy time the tool opens the database, reads the current version from its tracking table, sorts the migration files, and applies only the missing ones in order, updating the version as it goes. If a migration fails part-way, it marks the version dirty and refuses to proceed until a human resolves it.

scenes.heading: Embedding migrations in the binary
scenes.narration: With Go's embed.FS, you compile the migration directory straight into the binary and feed it to golang-migrate through the iofs source. The app then migrates itself with no external files to lose. Notice the Up call is guarded with errors-Is against ErrNoChange, because when there's nothing pending, that error just means the database is already up to date — so re-running is safe.

scenes.text: Rolling deploys run old and new code together, so migrate additively first — expand, then contract.
scenes.narration: In a rolling deploy, old and new code run at the same time, so every schema change must be backward compatible. The safe pattern is expand then contract: add a nullable column before the code that writes it, and only drop a column after all code stops using it. Never ship a migration the currently-running code can't tolerate.

scenes.text: Run migrations once per deploy as a pre-rollout gate; prefer roll-forward over destructive down migrations.
scenes.narration: So run migrations exactly once per deploy as a pre-rollout gate, not from every racing replica. Use non-transactional migrations for statements like CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. And in production, prefer a roll-forward fix over a destructive down migration, which can permanently lose data.
